gobekli-tepe.title: Architecture at human scale.
gobekli-tepe.intro: Two close views move from the overall monument to the architectural details that make Göbekli Tepe legible as a built environment rather than an abstract archaeological icon.

images.label: Building B
images.title: Göbeklitepe Building B
images.caption: A round-plan building roughly 10 metres in diameter, with T-shaped limestone pillars arranged around the wall and two central monoliths. Fox reliefs appear on the inward-facing sides of the central pillars.
images.alt: Round-plan Building B at Göbekli Tepe with T-shaped limestone pillars
images.creator: Dosseman

images.label: Building D
images.title: Göbeklitepe Building D
images.caption: The best-preserved monumental enclosure at the site. Its two central pillars survive to about 5.5 metres and carry anthropomorphic details including arms, hands, belts and loincloths.
images.alt: Building D at Göbekli Tepe with monumental central T-shaped pillars
images.creator: Dosseman

hattusa.title: Power in stone and landscape.
hattusa.intro: Hattusa is easier to understand when the royal citadel and the nearby rock sanctuary are seen together: political space inside the city and ritual space extending beyond it.

images.label: Royal citadel
images.title: Büyükkale, Buildings C and H
images.caption: Remains on Büyükkale, the royal citadel, where renewed excavation and radiocarbon work are refining the chronology of palace expansion and the Upper City.
images.alt: Stone remains of Buildings C and H on the Büyükkale citadel at Hattusa
images.creator: Carole Raddato

images.label: Yazılıkaya
images.title: Twelve Underworld Gods, Chamber B
images.caption: A procession of twelve male underworld deities carved into the rock of Chamber B at Yazılıkaya, the sanctuary that extends Hattusa's ritual landscape beyond the fortified city.
images.alt: Rock-cut procession of twelve underworld deities in Chamber B at Yazılıkaya
images.creator: Ywpark2003

catalhoyuk.title: The house as an archive.
catalhoyuk.intro: The strongest visual evidence at Çatalhöyük is interior: painted surfaces, platforms, installations and reconstructed spatial relationships show how architecture accumulated memory through repeated use.

images.label: Painted surface
images.title: Çatalhöyük wall painting
images.caption: A surviving wall painting now in the Konya Archaeological Museum. Painted and replastered surfaces were repeatedly renewed as part of the life histories of houses.
images.alt: Neolithic wall painting from Çatalhöyük displayed in the Konya Archaeological Museum
images.creator: Dosseman

images.label: Reconstruction
images.title: Reconstructed Çatalhöyük room
images.caption: A museum reconstruction using original finds in relative position to communicate the close relationship between roof-entry architecture, interior platforms and below-floor burial practices.
images.alt: Reconstructed Neolithic room from Çatalhöyük in the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations
images.creator: Dosseman

arslantepe.title: Power before writing.
arslantepe.intro: Arslantepe's political system becomes unusually tangible when the decorated palace interior is read together with its architectural plan: ideology, controlled movement and administration occupy the same built complex.

images.label: Painted authority
images.title: Palatial wall paintings from Arslantepe
images.caption: Painted surfaces from the late fourth-millennium palatial complex, now displayed in Malatya. Monumental architecture at Arslantepe communicated authority through images as well as through access and administration.
images.alt: Wall paintings from the fourth-millennium Arslantepe palatial complex displayed in Malatya
images.creator: Dosseman

images.label: Spatial administration
images.title: Plan of the Period VI A palace complex
images.caption: A plan reproduced from on-site interpretation of the 3350–3000 BCE palatial complex. The interconnected rooms make the institutional scale of circulation, storage and controlled access easier to read than isolated finds alone.
images.alt: Plan of the late fourth-millennium palace complex at Arslantepe
images.creator: Ingeborg Simon

gordion.title: Monument, burial and pattern.
gordion.intro: Gordion's elite world is visible at two very different scales: royal tumuli reshape the landscape, while coloured pebble mosaics turn geometric pattern into architecture inside the citadel.

images.label: Royal necropolis
images.title: Tumulus MM and Tumulus P
images.caption: Two eighth-century BCE burial mounds rise beside the citadel. Tumulus MM, left, preserves the great wooden chamber conventionally called the Midas Mound; Tumulus P, right, belonged to another wealthy Phrygian burial.
images.alt: Tumulus MM and Tumulus P rising from the plain beside Gordion
images.creator: Archaeologist1950

images.label: Pebble mosaic
images.title: Phrygian geometric mosaic
images.caption: A coloured pebble pavement from Gordion. The dense geometric vocabulary echoes the patterned world of Phrygian textiles and shows that visual display was embedded in architectural surfaces as well as portable luxury objects.
images.alt: Geometric Phrygian pebble mosaic from Gordion displayed in the Gordion Museum
images.creator: Dosseman

troy.title: One mound, incompatible scales of memory.
troy.intro: Two panoramic views place different archaeological Troys side by side: an Early Bronze Age megaron embedded in the citadel sequence and a sanctuary that reused the lower city centuries later. The site is easier to understand when continuity and reuse are visible at once.

images.label: Early Bronze Age
images.title: Megaron within the citadel sequence
images.caption: A panoramic view of a megaron built against the citadel wall in the Troy II–III sequence. The building preserves the architectural world that Schliemann cut through while searching for a much later Homeric city.
images.alt: Panoramic view of an Early Bronze Age megaron and citadel wall at Troy
images.creator: Dosseman

images.label: Greek and Roman reuse
images.title: Sanctuary over the Bronze Age lower city
images.caption: The sanctuary developed within an area cut into the ruins of Troy VI–VII and remained in use through Hellenistic and Roman phases. Later Ilion did not simply sit above Troy; it actively occupied and reinterpreted its archaeological landscape.
images.alt: Panoramic view of the sanctuary area at Troy with surviving stone foundations
images.creator: Dosseman
